title: The Bigfoot files don't prove Sasquatch exists. These Oklahomans still want to believe.
excerpt: Researcher DW Lee brought a thermal drone and field gear to a Hulbert library as federal "Bigfoot files" put Sasquatch back in the headlines.
content:
HULBERT, Okla. -

Bigfoot believers, skeptics and the simply curious filled the Hulbert Community Library on Tuesday to learn how modern researchers hunt for Sasquatch.

The timing is no accident. Newly released federal “Bigfoot files” have put the legend back in the headlines.

Field gear, not campfire stories

Researcher DW Lee brought a thermal drone, audio recorders and drop boxes built to sit in the woods and record for days.

Lee said the drone is flown over areas to look for thermal signatures. A thermal drop box can be left out for up to 27 hours, he said, and the audio recorders can run three to four days, depending on the battery.

Lee is executive director of the Mid-America Bigfoot Research Center. He said his first encounter came near a creek in Stilwell, where he and his daughter smelled something like dead fish before he saw a head and shoulders pop up over the creek bed. Lee said he has served in the Army and had a night vision scope with him.

“And I stood there, and I was like, did I just see what I thought I saw?” Lee said.

Believers share their stories

Brenda Carey, who sells Bigfoot-themed crafts such as coffee cups and T-shirts at festivals, calls herself somewhere between a skeptic and a believer. She said she has gone to Bigfoot events for about six or seven years.

Carey said a night camping at the Mena, Arkansas, Bigfoot festival is why. She said she and her husband were the only campers that year, and they heard coyotes before something else.

“And then we heard a sound we didn’t recognize, and that went on for about an hour or so, and it quit,” Carey said.

She said they heard a scream the next morning and she recorded it. She described it as “a very high pitch,” unlike anything they had heard before.

Owen Mitchell of Locust Grove said his story began in high school, when his little brother ran screaming out of the woods about a white creature. Years later, Mitchell said, he opened the door of his travel trailer late one night and saw a silhouette behind his cousin’s house.

“And it just walked really quickly and silently across,” Mitchell said.

He said he later measured a nearby tree and estimated the figure stood about 8 feet tall. If Bigfoot is out there, Mitchell said, it is on its own schedule, and if the creatures want to be known, “they’ll make themselves known.”

What the “Bigfoot files” say

The files include three historical records: a 1982 Forest Service investigation of tracks in the Umatilla National Forest, which spans northeast Oregon and southeast Washington; a hunter’s account of large tracks in the Montana snow in the 1940s; and a 2003 newspaper clipping about hundreds of footprints at a Montana sawmill.

The files do not confirm that Sasquatch exists, but they show the U.S. government took field reports seriously enough in the 1980s to dedicate taxpayer resources to casting tracks and documenting them.

In the 1982 memo, Forest Service wildlife biologist Rodney L. Johnson wrote that the tracks “appear very natural” and that, if they were faked, “someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail.” But he concluded they were made by something other than a 300-pound-plus, two-footed being. He cited several reasons, including that the stride did not change with the slope of the trail. Plaster casts were made of tracks at two sites.

A U.S. Border Patrol agent, Joel Hardin, who examined the same tracks, wrote in a separate memo that they were “a very clever attempt to perpetrate a hoax.”

In the Montana account, written in 1980, hunter Leo Kinney described following large tracks in the snow after finding the remains of an elk he and three others had planned to pack out. They decided they were not anxious to catch up to whatever made them, and Kinney wrote that they “could feel chills running up and down our backs.”

The 2003 clipping from the Clark Fork Valley Press in Plains, Montana, reported that 87-year-old Jim Rohweder found hundreds of large footprints near his sawmill after a snowfall. “If someone played a hoax, they did a pretty good job,” neighbor Bob Mesing told the newspaper.

“Skeptical both ways”

Carey said she hasn’t read the files yet, but their lack of proof does not change her mind.

“Every urban legend has an ounce of truth. So there’s something there. We just haven’t seen it or figured it out,” Carey said.

Lee said he suspects there is more the government hasn’t released, adding that “there’s got to be more information out there that they just haven’t released.” He also said about half the evidence people send him doesn’t hold up, in part because some people want “15 minutes of fame.”

But he said doubt has to cut both ways.

“Well, if you’re going to be skeptical, you got to be skeptical both ways,” Lee said.

Lee said the Oklahoma Bigfoot Symposium will be in Stilwell the second week of March with new speakers and thermal cameras running.
